title: Deliverable Format Follows Purpose
excerpt: Deliverable format follows audience and use. Creative Navy treats deliverables as composed artefacts whose level of context depends on what the recipient needs to do with them.
metaDescription: How Creative Navy calibrates deliverable format to audience, use, evidence transfer and implementation needs rather than convention.
summary: This page defines Creative Navy's principle that a deliverable should be formatted according to its recipient and intended use. It distinguishes memory-anchor artefacts for aligned teams from explanatory artefacts that must travel beyond the core team, and records examples from engagements where format, context and reasoning were deliberately composed.
definition: Deliverable format follows purpose means that the form, depth and structure of a deliverable are determined by who must receive it and what they need to do with it, not by agency convention or template habit.
keyFacts: The appropriate form of a deliverable depends on the recipient and the action the recipient needs to take.
For a small aligned team that participated in the discussions, a deliverable can act as a short memory anchor.
For recipients outside the core team, the same content needs more context, reasoning and explanation because understanding must be built rather than recalled.
The common failure mode is an unconsidered middle: a format filled in by convention that serves neither aligned participants nor uninitiated readers.
Workshops are described as the primary vector for knowledge transfer, with deliverables acting as reference documents that follow from them.
Many modelling deliverables create most of their value during preparation, because organising and prioritising the information builds the team's capacity to carry out the work.
In the Squaremind engagement, the Inform–Prevent–Correct framework was delivered as a mapped diagram because it needed to operate as a shared working reference during design reviews.

In the Topera engagement, Creative Navy scoped a full platform design at twenty-four one-week sprints, while the client commissioned three one-week sprints for a concept design; no build, testing, research or development handover took place.
In Assemblio, component documentation carried reasoning as well as specification, and the documented components were adopted by developers; the product ships as the design delivered.

In the maritime VTS engagement, a client engineer used documented reusable contracts to build a working validation-and-correction view in the client's frontend development sandbox without additional screen specification from Creative Navy.
bodyMarkdown:
## Deliverable format is determined by recipient and use

Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

Deliverable format follows purpose when the form of the artefact is determined by who needs to receive it and what that recipient needs to do with it. Format is not determined by convention. A persona, journey map, cognitive-load model, requirements table, decision record, diagram or design file can be appropriate or inappropriate depending on whether it needs to remind an aligned team, educate an uninitiated reader, support implementation, preserve a decision trail, or allow another party to check the work.

This principle changes the role of documentation in Creative Navy's design work. Workshops are the primary vector for knowledge transfer. Deliverables are reference documents that follow from the shared understanding created in those discussions. A document circulated by email cannot create the same shared understanding as a workshop in which the relevant design reasoning is developed and tested with the people who will use it.

## Short deliverables can be sufficient for an aligned team

A deliverable for a small, aligned team that participated in the discussions generating an insight can be a memory anchor. The document does not need to rebuild the reasoning from first principles because the core understanding already exists in the room. Its job is to recall shared understanding, not to create it.

In that situation, the best format can be short and simple. A persona can be thirty words and omit a name, hobbies, family status, demographics and other biographical details if those details have no bearing on design decisions in the project. The point of the persona is not to resemble a conventional persona template. The point is to preserve only the distinctions that matter for the decisions the team has to make.

A complex deliverable can be counterproductive for an aligned team. It can turn off stakeholders, consume time that does not add value, and obscure the specific operational distinctions the team already understands. In this setting, the useful deliverable is not the most complete artefact. It is the smallest artefact that reliably recalls the shared understanding created through discussion.

## Travelling deliverables must carry reasoning, not only conclusions

A deliverable that must travel beyond the core team needs a different format. The same content requires more context when the reader did not participate in the discussions that produced it. The deliverable has to explain not only what something is, but why it is that way, how it works in a specific situation, and what would have to change for it to be different.

For an uninitiated reader, understanding must be built rather than recalled. A deliverable that travels to developers, stakeholders, future reviewers, third-party suppliers or people not yet selected for the work must carry reasoning alongside specification. It must show the causal structure behind the decision, not just the surface of the decision.

Good pain-point documentation illustrates the distinction. A statement such as users experience time pressure is not actionable on its own. Useful documentation explains why the time pressure exists, how it manifests, what generates it, how users deal with it, and what it means for design decisions. If errors produce cascading resolution work that creates time debt mid-task, the design must address that underlying factor rather than the surface expression of time pressure.

## The unconsidered middle is the common deliverable failure mode

The failure mode in many agency deliverables is an unconsidered middle. The artefact is filled in according to a format rather than composed for an audience. It is too heavy to serve an aligned team efficiently and too thin to educate a reader who was not involved in the work.

Personas commonly show this failure mode when they include hobbies, family status, age and other details that have no bearing on how the user interacts with the system. Pain points show the same failure when they are listed in vague terms without explaining the underlying mechanism. A deliverable that says users experience time pressure but does not explain why the pressure arises cannot guide design decisions.

A composed deliverable is defined as much by what it declines to carry as by what it carries. Removing unsupported or irrelevant material is not a reduction in rigour. It is a decision about what the recipient needs in order to act correctly.

## Modelling artefacts often create value during preparation

Many modelling deliverables create much of their value during preparation rather than in the final artefact. Personas, journey maps, cognitive-load models and similar modelling forms require the team to organise information, process it at depth, prioritise distinctions and create hierarchy. That work builds the capability to carry out the rest of the engagement.

The artefact can still be useful, but it is not always the main point. The process of preparing the model changes what the team understands and what it can decide. This is why Creative Navy structures engagements around workshops first and documentation second. The deliverable follows the knowledge-transfer process rather than replacing it.

## Squaremind used a diagram because the Inform–Prevent–Correct structure had to be navigable

In the Squaremind engagement, Creative Navy introduced the Inform–Prevent–Correct framework to organise design work on the patient scanning interface. The framework had three layers, Inform, Prevent and Correct, applied recursively across every step of the scan flow. Each Correct event generated a sub-cycle for the recovery path.

The format decision mattered. A prose description could have communicated the concept, but it could not have served as a working reference during design reviews. It could not have been walked through step by step against the scan flow, and it could not have been handed to the client as an artefact for evaluating design decisions independently.

The diagram format made the Inform–Prevent–Correct architecture a working instrument. Both Creative Navy and the client could point at specific steps in the flow and examine what Inform required there, what Prevent needed to address, what happened if Correct was triggered, and what the system needed to do next. The diagram externalised the logic in a form the client could follow and challenge, even though the client consisted of two technical founders with no prior UX vocabulary.

The same Squaremind engagement also used design education content in each design presentation. The presentations explained the user behaviour patterns that made the design necessary, not only what the design did. For a small founding team with no prior design vocabulary, this changed what the presentation did: it gave the client vocabulary and understanding for evaluating options on the same terms Creative Navy used.

## Topera shows that a composed deliverable also excludes work deliberately

Topera was a cross-organisational project management platform concept design delivered across three one-week sprints. Creative Navy scoped a full design of the platform at twenty-four one-week sprints and put that estimate to the client before the engagement began. The client commissioned three one-week sprints as a concept design. The twenty-four-sprint figure was Creative Navy's professional estimate of full scope, not a measured comparison between two pieces of work.

The first decision in the Topera engagement was what the artefact was for. Its job was to be legible to people deciding whether the platform should exist. The available evidence records that Topera's team was pleased with the concept design and took it to show stakeholders. No stakeholder response, decision, commitment or funding event is known to Creative Navy.

The Topera concept design included a complete information architecture, including areas not implemented in the MVP but designed to appear as future extension points. It included four complete UI style directions for the same screen, including light and dark treatments. It also included designed states rather than only screens: hover, selected, empty, expanded, collapsed, read-only, error and validation-failure states across the surfaces.

The same composed deliverable excluded research, testing, a decision record and implementation work. No research of any kind took place. Nothing was tested with anyone. No record of client choices exists. Nothing was built and no development handover took place.

The data import flow in Topera was designed around failure rather than success. Per-row validation errors named the field and the fault. A separate duplicate-detection step listed colliding identifiers and offered an explicit choice between importing as new data and importing to overwrite. These were designed screens rather than error toasts. In a concept design, spending limited time on the duplicate-collision screen was a format decision about what the concept needed to demonstrate.

## AIT used retained iterations and a scoped prototype to support absent readers

In the AIT engagement, Creative Navy delivered five generations of wireframes for a European manufacturer of residential and commercial heat pumps. Superseded wireframe sets were retained in the file and banner-marked as discarded, with each discarded set pointing to the current iteration. The file was organised so that a reader who was not in the room could distinguish the live design from historical material.

The clickable prototype was deliberately scoped to one flow rather than spread across the product. The prototype covered the scenario-editing flow because it was the most complex and contested interaction, and because rotary-knob operation would be most laborious there. The format decision concentrated prototype effort where interaction uncertainty was highest.

## MDU shows a deliverable addressed to an audience not yet selected

The MDU was a ship motion monitoring system whose bridge interface Creative Navy designed. The manufacturer is not named. The design was not handed to a chosen implementer. Creative Navy explained the design to every third-party development agency the manufacturer was still choosing between, so that each could pitch its services on a common understanding of the delivered design.

This is a clear case of format following recipient. A deliverable addressed to an audience that has not been selected cannot be a memory anchor for an aligned team. It has to carry its own reasoning to readers with no shared history.

The companion artefact was a screen-by-screen requirements table. It paired module, screen, content, user actions and priority with Creative Navy's open questions and the manufacturer's answers and comments. The table functioned as a collaborative device for preserving what each screen required and what remained unresolved.

## Assemblio and Egma show reasoning and operating capability in handover

For Assemblio, Creative Navy's component documentation carried reasoning as well as specification. The documentation explained why a component was the way it was, not only what it was. Handover used a combination of formats, but the specific mix is not recorded and should not be reconstructed.

The Assemblio components Creative Navy documented were adopted by developers. Creative Navy compared the shipped interface against the delivered designs, and the product ships as the design that was delivered. This is evidence that the design survived development. It is not evidence of development speed, development cost, defect rate or product quality.

For Egma, the Dubai-based ophthalmic lens manufacturer whose B2B ordering platform Egma Order Creative Navy designed, the artefact was a design file and the handover was a training session in operating it. Creative Navy taught the client's developers to measure padding and gaps with a modifier key, jump from any instance to its main component and inspect every state, sample colour values, bulk-export the icon set as SVG, and use a plugin listing every place a component variant had been used.

The Egma design file retained discarded explorations on purpose so the record of what had been tried stayed navigable to someone who was not in the room. The design system was also composed as reasoning: responsive breakpoints were handed over as negotiable, while gutter rules were not.

## Schone and Raymarine used different deliverable forms for different readers

The Schone Airspace Group engagement produced twenty-five UX decision records. Each record carried decision context, resolved direction, two named rejected alternatives with the reason each was rejected, operator actions and system responses, a concrete operational instance, the design consequence and trade-off stated as a cost, the engineering interface it depends on, and explicit acceptance conditions. These decision records were composed for a reader who was not in the room.

The same Schone Airspace Group handover included a machine-readable package alongside the written specification. The package included a design token file, a component register, a screen register and an acceptance ledger, versioned together so component variants, screen content and state decisions could be checked against one release index. This was a deliverable form composed for a system rather than a person. The registers and records are engagement record, not outcome evidence.

The Raymarine engagement on its next-generation fixed-mount VHF produced three deliverable forms for three readers. The component contract was composed for an implementer who was not in the room and needed to know what each state must be true of. Each component definition included purpose, information required, state variants, valid actions, focus and disabled treatment, priority behaviour and dependencies.

The Raymarine decision register was composed for a future reviewer. It contained thirty-two recorded UX decisions, each carrying the trigger, the selected rule, the main competing option not carried forward, a disposition distinguishing a settled UX decision from one awaiting engineering, compliance or further test, and traceability to the specification that held it.

The third Raymarine form was a change-control rule written for a team that did not yet exist. It named four proposals that would reopen a recorded UX decision: remapping the channel encoder, removing routine recipient confirmation, merging incident statuses, or permitting automatic network-initiated radio actions. The rule also set boundaries on what presentation could vary without inverting the meaning of a physical control, altering a calling transaction outcome or removing the need for explicit incident resolution. The registers are engagement record, not outcome evidence.

## The maritime VTS engagement used contracts that had to educate engineers across stacks

For a European vendor of maritime traffic monitoring, inland navigation and communications software for port authorities, coastal administrations and waterway operators, the contract specification had to educate rather than remind. The audience was the client's own engineers across multiple frontend stacks, and those engineers had not been in the discussions.

The frontend architecture lead had established that the portfolio spanned browser products and dedicated communication terminals. A single code component library could not be assumed to run unchanged in each. Component documentation therefore had to include states, transitions and failure treatment rather than spacing and colour alone.

Each reusable contract carried a minimum specification: purpose and eligibility including explicit non-use cases; information model with source of truth, identifiers, timestamps, unknown values and permissions; behaviour with triggers, transitions, keyboard focus, interruption and recovery; visual portrayal including accessible text, responsive density and night mode; and quality evidence with accepted scenarios, reviewer and remaining exceptions.

The adoption exercise tested whether the format worked. A client engineer who was not a member of the design team built a working validation-and-correction view for the electronic reporting product in the client's own frontend development sandbox, using twelve documented patterns and two domain adaptations, with no additional screen specification from Creative Navy.

## The handheld command-and-control engagement separated doctrine from a checkable specification

For a European manufacturer of uncrewed systems, including one-way effectors, and the tactical command-and-control software that operates them, Creative Navy led and co-authored two deliverables with the client's design team. The engagement covered interface structure, task behaviour, information priority and the clarity of operator control. It did not extend to autonomy, control algorithms, autonomous safety behaviour, the datalink, the effector, targeting logic, certification or weapons-review activity. Creative Navy designed the surface through which a human supervises the system; it did not design the system.

The operational doctrine was composed for a reader who was not in the room. It was a decision model for what a handheld may show at all, structured around five functions: Aviate, Navigate and Execute the Mission as the primary trio, with Command and Control and Manage Contingencies as cross-cutting functions applying continuously rather than in sequence. The model was adapted from published NASA, FAA and EASA uncrewed-aircraft human-factors guidance rather than copied from any one framework. Each function carried a primary operator question, supporting questions, the information required to answer them, and its relationship to the other four.

The touch-sizing specification was composed for a reader who would argue with it. It had three columns: the standard, MIL-STD-1472 plus gloved-touch research; the field's practice, where no fielded ground control station abides by it; and the proposed middle ground of consequence tiers. It included eleven numbered references spanning MIL-STD-1472, FAA human factors design standards, WCAG 2.2 and NASA ground-control-station guidelines. It also recorded a named open dependency, the unresolved reference glove, with the tiers assuming the heavier case. T3 was labelled a hypothesis in the deliverable itself and recorded as sitting in an untested band to be validated.

A specification written to be checked by someone who might disagree is a different artefact from a specification written to be followed. That difference is a format decision about the recipient's expected action.

## Evidence boundaries for deliverable-format claims

The examples on this page are engagement records and documented case evidence. They support the claim that Creative Navy composes deliverable formats according to audience and purpose. They do not establish that any deliverable type guarantees a project result.

Topera has strict boundaries. Nothing was built, no product existed, no deployment took place, no users or pilot are recorded, and no development handover took place. The twenty-four-sprint figure is a professional estimate of full scope, not a compression claim. The stakeholder showing is not evidence of traction, validation, approval, interest or momentum.

Assemblio has a narrower positive outcome. The documented components were adopted, and the product ships as the design delivered. No claim is made about development speed, cost, defect rates, training, revenue or funding.

The maritime VTS adoption exercise is stronger than a document-completion claim because a client engineer built a working validation-and-correction view in the client's frontend development sandbox without additional screen specification from Creative Navy. It remains an adoption exercise, not a measured business or operational outcome.

The handheld command-and-control deliverables were led and co-authored with the client's design team. The doctrine and touch-sizing specification are design documents, not safety determinations. The T3 sizing tier was a hypothesis, not a validated result.

## Related pages

The Squaremind, Topera, AIT, MDU, Assemblio, Egma, Schone Airspace Group, Raymarine, maritime VTS and tactical handheld command-and-control pages provide the case-specific records behind the examples. The evidence standards pages on what Creative Navy does not claim and what Creative Navy has measured provide the broader calibration rules for outcome and evidence language.
